claims.text: At an event the author heard misconceptions about open source that are increasingly common among developers and buyers who use it every day without having grown up in its culture.
claims.quote: without having grown up in its culture

claims.text: Open source is a copyright licence: the holder uses the right to control copying to grant copying, use, change and sharing on stated terms; it is not the absence of copyright.
claims.quote: It is a copyright licence. It is not the absence of copyright.

claims.text: GNU was announced in 1983, the Free Software Foundation founded in 1985, and in 1989 the first GPL made copyleft a licence: sharing as a condition, which critics called viral.
claims.quote: copyleft, a clever inversion of copyright that makes sharing a condition

claims.text: The term open source was proposed by Christine Peterson in February 1998 after Netscape released its browser's source; the OSI was founded that month by Bruce Perens and Eric Raymond with a definition from the Debian guidelines.
claims.quote: It was proposed by Christine Peterson at a meeting in February 1998, after Netscape decided to release its browser's source

claims.text: The correction to the author's own shorthand: Linux did not leave the GPL for pragmatism; it adopted GPL version 2 in 1992 and has stayed there, and the pragmatism was in the attitude.
claims.quote: Linux adopted GPL version 2 in 1992 and has stayed there.

claims.text: The repositories behind this site are Apache 2.0 for code and Creative Commons for writing; Apache 2.0 adds an explicit patent grant, which matters more than it looks.
claims.quote: The repositories behind this site are Apache 2.0 for code and Creative Commons for writing

claims.text: The author once thought the most open thing was not to licence at all; it is the opposite, because with no licence ordinary copyright applies and all rights are reserved.
claims.quote: With no licence, ordinary copyright applies and all rights are reserved

claims.text: A small group of maintainers decides what goes into a project; contributions are reviewed, tested, signed off and often refused, and anybody can fork their own copy but nobody can change yours.
claims.quote: Anybody can fork a project and change their own copy; nobody can change yours without you.

claims.text: The control over an open source project is real; it is just visible, which is a strength, because you can see exactly who decides and what they accepted.
claims.quote: The control is real. It is just visible, which is a strength

claims.text: Apart from a very small minority of popular projects, almost every open source project is run by a small number of people, which is the normal shape of it, not a failure.
claims.quote: That is not a failure of open source; it is the normal shape of it.

claims.text: Open source is neither dramatically more nor less secure than proprietary software, because openness is not the metric; the metric is whether somebody had the time, and was paid, to review it.
claims.quote: Open source is not dramatically more secure or less secure than proprietary software, because openness is not the metric.

claims.text: Black Duck's annual analysis finds open source in almost all commercial codebases; closing a product does not close its dependencies, it only hides them.
claims.quote: Closing a product does not close its dependencies; it only hides them.

claims.text: Tidelift's 2024 maintainer survey found around 60% of maintainers describing themselves as unpaid hobbyists, and paid maintainers markedly more likely to implement recommended security practices.
claims.quote: around 60% of maintainers describing themselves as unpaid hobbyists

value.unit: percent of maintainers describing themselves as unpaid hobbyists

claims.text: The result is a tragedy of the commons: powerful software used by millions, and organisations that pay a consultant to customise it rather than the people who wrote it and would do it better.
claims.quote: organisations that will pay a consultant to customise it or work out how to use it rather than paying the people who wrote it and would do it better

claims.text: The xz utils backdoor, found in March 2024, hit a library under much of Linux maintained by one person; an attacker spent years earning trust and shipped a backdoor in two releases before an engineer noticed slow SSH logins.
claims.quote: shipped a backdoor in two releases before an engineer noticed SSH logins were slow

claims.text: The lesson of xz is not that open source is unsafe but that mission-critical software was maintained by somebody with almost no time and no money, and we should be paying those individuals.
claims.quote: The lesson is not that open source is unsafe.

claims.text: Funding maintainers never worked partly because they want to write code, not run services, and the workflows to do both were not practical; with agents, they are becoming practical.
claims.quote: With agents, I think they are becoming practical.

claims.text: Model weights are like a compiled application: you can run and fine-tune them but not build them from scratch, so the labs that now say open weights rather than open source are right.
claims.quote: Model weights are like a compiled application

claims.text: The OSI's Open Source AI Definition requires the code used to train and run a model, its parameters, and enough information about the training data that a skilled person could build a substantially equivalent system.
claims.quote: enough information about the training data that a skilled person could build a substantially equivalent system

claims.text: Open-weight models are one of the largest economic advantages a company can have, because they can be run and built on inside your own environment; they are a different thing, called by the right name.
claims.quote: open-weight models are one of the largest economic advantages a company can have

claims.text: The question about open-weight models is how a tool is used and by whom; Metasploit made exploitation dramatically easier and the world adjusted, though some capabilities should not be released.
claims.quote: Metasploit made exploitation dramatically easier when it appeared, and the world adjusted.

claims.text: Even open source has to be hosted somewhere and distributed through somebody, which is itself a point of control; the idea of a free-for-all without any control is not true.
claims.quote: even open source has to be hosted somewhere and distributed through somebody, which is itself a point of control

claims.text: The power of open source has nothing to do with contributions: it is that you are not locked in, and can read it, run it, fix it and move it if the company behind it is sold, changes licence or disappears.
claims.quote: The power is that you are not locked in.

claims.text: With open source you get the whole development and technology workflow: the history, the tests, the build and the reasoning in the commits, as valuable as the code.
claims.quote: the history, the tests, the build, the reasoning in the commits, all of which are as valuable as the code

claims.text: There is no sovereignty without open source: a European supplier today is one acquisition away from not being one, and only control that survives a change of owner counts.
claims.quote: a European supplier today is one acquisition away from not being one

claims.text: open-source.sgit.ai is the longer version, with the position, the corrected history, the licences used, a vendor stress test and the funding question; its first lesson is that open source is not free, somebody is always paying.
claims.quote: open source is not free, somebody is always paying for it.

claims.text: The article is not legal advice; licences are legal instruments, so read the licence and ask a lawyer when it matters.
claims.quote: It is not legal advice.

claims.text: The history is the short version; earlier permissive licences existed alongside the GPL, and the full story with corrections and sources is on open-source.sgit.ai.
claims.quote: Earlier permissive licences existed alongside the GPL

claims.text: The maintainer figures are surveys: Tidelift's 60% is how maintainers describe themselves, and the share who say they are unpaid for their work is lower in the same survey.
claims.quote: The maintainer figures are surveys.

claims.text: Contributions do happen; the claim is that they are not the point and not the norm, not that they never matter.
claims.quote: The claim is that they are not the point and not the norm, not that they never matter.

claims.text: The article comes from a voice memo of 12 October 2026 after an event; where the memo had the history slightly wrong, the agent corrected it from sources and the corrections are in the text.
claims.quote: where my memo had the history slightly wrong, the agent corrected it from sources and the corrections are in the text
